learnings.title: "How do you use AI in your day-to-day work?"
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
This is now a standard opener, and it is not small talk. The interviewer is checking three things: that you have actually used these tools on real code, that you know where they fail, and that your judgement did not get outsourced along with the typing.

## The shape of a good answer

Name the work, not the tool. "I use Claude Code" says nothing; "I use it to do the mechanical 80% of a migration and I review every hunk" says what you actually do.

> "It is fastest for me on three things: scaffolding something I have written twenty times before, doing a mechanical change across a lot of files, and getting oriented in a codebase I do not know. It is slowest — actively negative — on anything where the hard part is deciding what to build. I still read every line before it lands, because I am the one who has to defend it in review."

## Where it genuinely wins

| Task | Why it fits |
| --- | --- |
| Boilerplate and scaffolding | You know exactly what correct looks like, so review is fast |
| Mechanical refactors across files | The change is repetitive; the risk is missing a site, not judgement |
| Tests for existing code | Coverage of the cases you would have skipped at 6pm |
| Reading unfamiliar code | "Where does auth happen in this repo" beats grep for the first hour |
| The blank page | A first draft you disagree with is easier than nothing |
| One-off scripts | The migration, the data fix, the log parse — read once, run once |

## Where it costs you

- **Design decisions.** It will produce a confident architecture with no idea of your constraints, your team, or what shipped last quarter.
- **Anything subtly stateful.** Race conditions, [cache invalidation](/system-design/405), effect dependencies — plausible code that is wrong under load.
- **Unfamiliar territory.** You cannot review what you do not understand, so the speed-up is borrowed against a debt you pay in production.
- **Small, precise edits.** Describing a three-line change often takes longer than making it.

## The honest framing to say out loud

> "The bottleneck moved. Writing code is faster; reviewing, verifying and deciding are not, so those became the job. If I let generation outrun review, I have just produced more code I do not understand."

## Answers that lose points

- "I do not use it." Reads as incuriosity, whatever you meant.
- "It writes most of my code now" — with no mention of review or verification.
- Tool-listing with no story about a real change you shipped.
- Blaming the model for a bug you shipped. It was your commit.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Give an example where it saved you real time."** — Have one ready with numbers: the task, the shape of the change, roughly how long each way.
- **"Where has it burned you?"** — Have one of those too. A candidate with no failure story has not used it seriously.
- **"How do you stop juniors leaning on it too hard?"** — Review the reasoning, not just the diff; make people explain code they submitted.

learnings.title: Reviewing AI-written code — what to check first
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
The interesting question is not whether the code works. It is which failure modes survive a normal review, because those are the ones that reach production.

## What survives a careless review

AI-written code is **syntactically clean, stylistically consistent and confidently wrong** in specific ways. It looks reviewed already, which is exactly the problem: your eye slides over it.

| Failure mode | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **Plausible API** | A method that should exist and does not, or the right name with the wrong signature |
| **Stale idiom** | Yesterday's pattern — a deprecated lifecycle, an old router API, a superseded config |
| **Silent edge cases** | Empty array, zero, `null`, the single-item case — handled in the happy path only |
| **Duplicated helper** | A new `formatDate` next to your three existing ones |
| **Over-abstraction** | A factory and two interfaces where a function was asked for |
| **Missing cleanup** | Listeners, intervals, subscriptions, `AbortController` — created, never removed |
| **Confident comments** | A comment that describes what the code was supposed to do |
| **Invented test** | A test that asserts the implementation rather than the behaviour, and passes trivially |

## The order to read in

1. **Does it belong here at all?** Right file, right layer, or a new module that should have been an addition to an existing one.
2. **Does it reuse what we have?** This is the most common miss, because the model only sees what it was shown.
3. **What happens at the edges?** Empty, one, many, null, error, slow, concurrent.
4. **What is the cleanup story?** Anything created must be destroyed.
5. **Is the test real?** Would it fail if you broke the behaviour? Delete a line of the implementation and check.
6. **Only then**: style, naming, types.

## The habit that actually works

**Run it before you read it, then read it as if a stranger wrote it** — because one did. If you cannot explain a line to someone else, it does not land. That rule alone catches most of the table above.

For a large generated change, review it in slices by concern rather than top-to-bottom: all the error handling, then all the state, then all the tests. Repetition is where a generated diff hides its one inconsistent hunk.

## The team-level version

- Generated code is **your** commit. Authorship and accountability do not transfer.
- A PR description should say what was generated and what you verified — not as a confession, as review guidance.
- Keep the diff small. A 2,000-line generated PR gets rubber-stamped; that is a property of humans, not of the code.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How is reviewing AI code different from reviewing a colleague's?"** — A colleague's code is wrong in ways that look wrong. This code is wrong in ways that look right, and it never says "I wasn't sure here".
- **"What do you check first?"** — Whether it duplicates something we already have, and what happens at the edges. Style is last; a formatter handles it.
- **"How do you keep quality up when volume goes up?"** — Smaller PRs, tests that would actually fail, and refusing to merge code nobody can explain.

learnings.title: Context engineering — why what you show beats what you ask
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
The single biggest quality lever is not the wording of the prompt. It is what the model can see when it answers.

## The rule

**A model cannot follow a convention it has never seen.** Ask for "a data table component" and you get a generic one. Show it the three components next door, your hooks, your token file and your test style, and you get one that fits — with no instructions about style at all.

Practically: point at the neighbours.

> "Add a `useInfiniteScroll` hook. Follow `src/hooks/useColumnWidths.js` for structure and JSDoc style, and `src/hooks/useKeyboardShortcuts.test.js` for the test shape."

## What is worth spending context on

| High value | Low value |
| --- | --- |
| The two or three files most like what you want | The whole repo |
| The exact error, with the stack trace | "It's broken" |
| The interface the code must satisfy | A prose description of the interface |
| A failing test | A description of the failure |
| The constraint that is not in the code ("this runs on the edge, no Node APIs") | Restating what the code obviously does |

The failing test is the strongest single input: it is unambiguous, machine-checkable, and it defines done.

## Project-level context beats per-prompt context

A `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` / `.cursorrules` at the repo root carries the things you would otherwise retype daily: the package manager, the test command, the layering rules, the "never commit without asking" rules, the patterns you have already rejected. Written once, applied every session — and it is reviewable, so the team agrees on it rather than each person keeping their own version in their head.

The same idea one level down: a short comment above a subtle function is context for the next reader *and* for the next generation pass.

## More context is not better

- **Irrelevant files dilute.** Twenty files where three would do makes the important ones proportionally less influential.
- **Stale context actively harms.** A deleted pattern still described in the rules file will be reproduced faithfully.
- **Contradictions are resolved arbitrarily.** If your rules file says one thing and the code next door does another, you cannot predict which wins.

Curate it like documentation, because that is what it is.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you get consistent output across a team?"** — Committed project rules plus pointing at exemplar files, so the conventions live in the repo rather than in individual prompting habits.
- **"What do you do when the answer keeps missing?"** — Stop rewording. Change the inputs: add the failing test, the real error, or the file it should have imitated.
- **"Is prompt engineering a skill you'd hire for?"** — Less than context engineering. Choosing what the model should see is the part that transfers.

learnings.title: When not to reach for it
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
Knowing where the tool stops is the part of the answer that separates a practitioner from an enthusiast.

## Do not reach for it when…

**The hard part is the decision.** Should this be one service or two? Do we support offline? Is this a product problem? A model will answer confidently, sourced from an average of the internet rather than from your constraints.

**You could not review the output.** A domain you do not know, a language you do not read, a security-sensitive path. Speed you cannot verify is a liability, and "it looked right" is not a review.

**The change is small and precise.** Renaming a variable, moving a line, fixing an off-by-one. Describing it costs more than doing it.

**Correctness is subtle and the failure is silent.** Concurrency, [cache invalidation](/system-design/405), floating-point money, timezone arithmetic, migrations. All are areas where plausible code passes tests and fails in production.

**The data cannot leave.** Customer records, credentials, private keys, anything under a contract that says where it may be processed. Know your organisation's rule before you paste, not after.

**You are learning it.** If the point of the task is to understand the thing, generating the answer removes the point. Use it as a tutor afterwards, not as a substitute.

## The tell that you have gone too far

You are debugging code you did not write, in a design you did not choose, and the fastest way forward is to delete it and start again. That has a cost, and it is the cost the honest version of this answer names.

## The counterweight

None of this means "use it for trivia only". The right framing:

> "I use it where I can verify the output quickly and where being wrong is cheap to detect. I do not use it where the failure is silent or the decision is mine to defend."

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Has it ever slowed you down?"** — Yes: a plausible refactor across a state machine that took longer to unpick than to write. The tell was that I stopped being able to explain the code.
- **"How do you handle the data-privacy side?"** — Know the policy, keep customer data out of prompts, prefer tooling approved for the repo, and treat pasting production data as an incident.
- **"Would you let it write your migration?"** — The scaffolding yes, the correctness no. That is a review-it-line-by-line change with a dry run against a copy.

learnings.title: Verification loops — hallucinated APIs and confident wrong refactors
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
The failure that costs teams real time is not obviously-broken code. It is code that is *nearly* right and reads as finished.

## The three shapes

**1 · The API that should exist.** A method with the right name and the wrong signature, an option that was proposed but never shipped, a package that does not exist. Usually caught by types or the first run — unless it is behind a rarely-taken branch.

**2 · The confident wrong refactor.** Mechanically correct across forty files, with one behavioural change in the middle: an early return dropped, an `await` added where the concurrency mattered, a `useEffect` dependency list "cleaned up". Tests pass. It surfaces a week later.

**3 · The fabricated explanation.** Asked why the code is slow, it gives a fluent, plausible mechanism that is not what is happening. This is the dangerous one, because it feels like understanding and it redirects your debugging.

## The loop that catches them

```
generate → run → read → check against the source of truth → then trust
```

- **Run it first.** Type-check, tests, the actual page. Free, fast, catches shape 1 almost entirely.
- **Diff-read a refactor by behaviour, not by file.** Ask "what did this change do?" for each hunk, and be suspicious of the hunks that look identical to the others — the odd one out is where the bug is.
- **Check claims against the docs**, not against the model. If an explanation of a framework behaviour matters, verify it in the source or the changelog. A version-specific claim is the highest-risk kind.
- **Make it prove the bug first.** A failing test before the fix means the fix is verified rather than asserted.
- **Ask for the uncertainty explicitly.** "Which parts of this are you unsure about?" produces a genuinely useful list surprisingly often.

## Guard rails that scale past you

- **Types on**, strict. The cheapest hallucination detector available.
- **CI that fails**, not warns: types, tests, lint, size budget.
- **A test that would fail.** Break a line of the implementation and confirm the new test goes red; a generated test that passes against a broken implementation is worse than no test.
- **Small commits.** A behavioural regression inside a 40-file refactor is found by `git bisect` only if the commits are separable.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you know the code is right?"** — The same way as any code: it runs, the tests would fail if it were wrong, and I can explain each line. The tool does not change the bar.
- **"What is a hallucination in practice?"** — Usually an API that ought to exist. The expensive version is a fluent explanation of a bug that is not the bug.
- **"How do you review a 40-file generated refactor?"** — By behaviour and by pattern: find the hunks that differ from their neighbours, and require a test that fails without the change.

learnings.title: Building AI features in a frontend — streaming, cancellation, cost
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
Interviewers increasingly ask you to design a feature that talks to a model. The frontend problems are specific and they are not about the model at all.

![Streaming UI — tokens, cancellation, and the states in between](/diagrams/sysdesign/ai-streaming-ui.svg)

## Why streaming is not optional

A model answer takes 2–20 seconds. Waiting for the whole thing gives you a spinner for ten seconds; streaming gives first text in a few hundred milliseconds. The perceived-latency difference is the entire feature.

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();

const res = await fetch("/api/chat", {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify({ messages }),
  signal: controller.signal,
});

const reader = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
let text = "";
while (true) {
  const { value, done } = await reader.read();
  if (done) break;
  text += value;
  setMessage(text); // batched by React; do not re-parse markdown per token
}
```

Transport: **SSE or a plain streamed `fetch` response**, not WebSocket. The traffic is one-directional per request and both survive proxies better. See [Real-time transports](/system-design/105).

## The states you must design

A model call has more states than "loading" and "done":

| State | UI |
| --- | --- |
| Queued | The request exists, no tokens yet — a thinking indicator, not a spinner on the whole page |
| Streaming | Partial text, a stop button, autoscroll that yields when the user scrolls up |
| Tool running | "Searching…" — the model is not producing text and the user must not think it hung |
| Complete | Actions appear: copy, retry, feedback |
| Stopped by user | Keep the partial output; it is often still useful |
| Failed mid-stream | Partial text plus a retry that does not lose it |
| Refused / empty | A real message, not an empty bubble |

**Cancellation is a first-class feature.** Users stop a bad answer constantly. Abort the fetch *and* tell the server, or you keep paying for tokens nobody will read.

## Rendering cost

Naively re-rendering a markdown parse of the whole message on every token is O(n²) and janks the tab by the third paragraph.

- Append to a plain text node while streaming; parse markdown on completion, or on a [throttle](/coding/14) (every ~100 ms).
- Memoise completed messages so a new token does not re-render the transcript.
- Virtualise long conversations.
- Handle incomplete syntax gracefully — a half-streamed code fence must not flash the raw backticks.

## Cost and abuse, which are frontend concerns too

- **Tokens are money.** Long context is charged on every turn; sending the entire transcript each time is a real bill. Trim or summarise older turns.
- **Rate limit and [debounce](/coding/13).** Never fire a model call per keystroke.
- **Never put the API key in the client.** Calls go through your own endpoint, which authenticates the user, enforces limits, and keeps the key server-side. A key in the bundle is a public key.
- **Optimistic UI has a different shape here.** You cannot predict the response, so what you show immediately is the user's own message and the pending state.

## Key takeaways

- Stream, or the feature feels broken; first token matters more than total time.
- Design the seven states, especially cancel, tool-running and mid-stream failure.
- Throttle the parse, memoise the transcript, virtualise the list.
- The key lives on the server; cost and rate limiting are part of the design.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"SSE or WebSocket?"** — SSE or a streamed fetch: one-directional, simpler, proxy-friendly. WebSocket only if the client also streams continuously.
- **"The user closes the tab mid-answer."** — Abort signals the server to stop generation; otherwise you pay for tokens into the void.
- **"How do you keep it fast on a long conversation?"** — Virtualise, memoise finished turns, parse on a throttle, and trim the context you resend.

learnings.title: Guardrails and evals — how you know the feature works
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
A normal feature is correct or it is not. A model feature has a distribution of outputs, so "it worked when I tried it" is not evidence and the interviewer knows it.

## Evals: tests for a non-deterministic system

An eval is a fixed set of inputs plus a way of scoring the outputs, run on every change to the prompt, the model or the retrieval.

1. **Build the set from real traffic.** Twenty to fifty cases beats a thousand invented ones: the common paths, the ones that broke, the adversarial ones, and the ones that should be refused.
2. **Score by what you can actually measure.** Exact match or a schema check where the output is structured; a rubric with an LLM judge where it is prose; a human pass on a small sample for the things neither catches.
3. **Freeze the set.** The value is comparability across versions. A new failure joins the set permanently.
4. **Run in CI.** A prompt edit is a code change, and it needs the same gate.

The point is not a score. It is that you can answer "did that change make it better?" with something other than a hunch.

## Guardrails

| Layer | Guard |
| --- | --- |
| Input | Length caps, rate limits, PII stripping, prompt-injection filtering on anything user- or web-supplied |
| Model | A system prompt that states scope, and refusal behaviour for out-of-scope requests |
| Output | Schema validation for structured output; never trust it as HTML |
| UI | Attribution and citations, an obvious "this can be wrong" affordance, and an easy correction path |
| Action | A human confirmation before anything that writes, spends or sends |

Two of those are non-negotiable on the frontend:

- **Never render model output as raw HTML.** It is untrusted input; treat it exactly like a user comment. Markdown, sanitised, links stripped or vetted — otherwise you have built an [XSS](/browser/158) injector that writes its own payloads.
- **Nothing irreversible without confirmation.** A model may propose a delete; a person approves it.

## Prompt injection, in one paragraph

Any text the model reads can contain instructions: a web page it fetched, a PDF a user uploaded, a comment in a repo. There is no complete fix. What works is architectural: keep retrieved content clearly separated from instructions, do not grant the model capabilities the current user does not have, and put a confirmation in front of every consequential action. Treat "the model was told to do it" as equivalent to "an anonymous user asked for it".

## What to monitor in production

- Latency to first token, and to completion.
- Refusal rate, empty-response rate, error rate by cause.
- Cost per conversation and per user.
- Thumbs-down rate, retries and edits after an answer — the strongest quality signals you get for free.
- A sampled log of real conversations that a human reads weekly. Nothing replaces this.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How would you test this?"** — A frozen eval set from real traffic, scored per dimension, run in CI on every prompt or model change, plus a weekly human read of sampled sessions.
- **"How do you handle a wrong answer?"** — Design for it: citations, an obvious correction path, and no irreversible action without confirmation. Then feed the failure into the eval set.
- **"What is prompt injection and how do you defend?"** — Untrusted text carrying instructions. Defend architecturally: least privilege, separation of content from instructions, and human confirmation before consequential actions.

learnings.title: The team questions — ownership, policy, licensing, security
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
Senior interviews move past your keyboard and ask how this works across a team of thirty. These are the four topics that come up.

## 1 · Ownership

**The person who merged it owns it.** Not the tool, not the reviewer. This has to be said explicitly, because "the AI wrote it" appears in incident reviews and it is never an acceptable line. Practically: if you cannot explain a line under questioning, it should not be in your PR.

## 2 · Review policy that survives the volume

Generation raises throughput on the writing side only, so the review queue becomes the constraint.

- **Cap PR size.** A 2,000-line PR is not reviewed, whoever wrote it.
- **Say what was verified**, not what was generated: "types pass, added a failing test first, manually checked the empty state".
- **Require a test that would fail.** The cheapest defence against confident-looking code.
- **No merges nobody can explain.** Make that a stated norm rather than an implied one.

## 3 · Licensing and provenance

Generated code can resemble training data, and some of that is copyleft. The realistic posture:

- Use tooling with an enterprise agreement and IP indemnification where your legal team requires it.
- Do not paste code from unknown sources into the repo, model-produced or not.
- Be more careful in a library you publish than in an internal app — distribution is what makes licence terms bite.
- Keep the policy written down and boring, so nobody has to guess.

## 4 · Security and data

- **Nothing secret in a prompt.** Credentials, customer records, private keys, unreleased material. Assume a prompt is logged somewhere.
- **Know which tools are approved** for which repos, and whether the vendor trains on your input.
- **The bill of materials still applies.** A model may suggest a package; you still check what it is, who maintains it, and how big it is. "The AI recommended it" is not a supply-chain review.
- **Generated infrastructure is still infrastructure.** A [Dockerfile](/system-design/112) or a Terraform plan gets the same review as hand-written config, because a wrong one is a public bucket.

## The answer that reads as senior

> "I treat it as a very fast junior with no memory and no accountability. It can produce a lot of plausible work; the team's job is unchanged — decide what to build, review what lands, and own it afterwards. What I would change process-wise is smaller PRs and stricter CI, because those are the two things that stop the extra volume turning into extra defects."

## Interview follow-ups

- **"A junior submits a PR they clearly did not write and cannot explain."** — Coach, do not merge. The rule is that authorship means accountability; ask them to walk through it, and treat the gaps as the learning.
- **"How do you stop AI-generated code degrading the codebase over time?"** — Convention files kept current, exemplar-driven reviews, duplication checks, and a size budget. Drift is the real risk, not any single PR.
- **"Would you use it on this codebase?"** — Ask what the policy is, what data is sensitive, and what the review norms are — that answer itself is the signal.

learnings.title: RAG for a frontend feature — retrieval, grounding, citations
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
"Ask our docs" is the most commonly requested AI feature and the most commonly botched. RAG — retrieval-augmented generation — is the pattern: **find the relevant text first, then ask the model to answer using only that**. Most of the work is retrieval, and almost none of it is prompting.

![RAG — retrieve, ground, stream, cite](/diagrams/sysdesign/rag-pipeline.svg)

## The pipeline

**Offline, once per document change**

1. **Chunk.** Split the source into passages. Chunk on structure — headings, sections — not on a fixed character count that cuts a table in half. 200–500 tokens with a little overlap is the usual starting point.
2. **Embed.** Turn each chunk into a vector, store it with its metadata: source URL, title, section, updated-at, and whatever access scope it belongs to.

**Per query**

3. **Retrieve.** Embed the question, take the nearest chunks — and run a keyword search alongside it. **Hybrid beats pure vector search**: semantic similarity is bad at exact identifiers, error codes and product names, which is what people actually search for.
4. **Rerank.** A cheap cross-encoder over the top ~50 to pick the best ~5. This is usually the single largest quality jump for the least work.
5. **Ground.** Put those chunks in the prompt with their ids, and instruct: answer from these, cite them, say you do not know if they do not cover it.
6. **Generate and stream**, with citations attached to the claims.

## What the frontend actually owns

- **Show the retrieval, not just the answer.** Sources listed, each clickable, highlighted at the passage that was used. It is the difference between a demo and something people trust.
- **Citations that survive streaming.** Tokens arrive before the source list is resolvable; render citation markers as placeholders and hydrate them, rather than letting raw `[3]` flash and then move the text.
- **A visible "no answer" state.** "I could not find this in the docs" is a *success*. Design it, or the model fills the gap with fluent invention.
- **The retrieval status.** "Searching…" then "Reading 5 sources" — a spinner during a two-second retrieval reads as a hang. Same states as any [streaming UI](/ai-dev/6).
- **Feedback per answer**, tied to the retrieved ids, so you learn whether the failure was retrieval or generation. Those are different bugs with different fixes.

## Where it goes wrong

| Symptom | Usual cause |
| --- | --- |
| Confident but wrong | Retrieval missed; the model answered from its own weights. Instruct it to refuse, and check whether the chunk was even in the top 50 |
| Right document, wrong part | Chunks too large, or no reranking |
| Cannot find an exact term | Pure vector search — add keyword/BM25 |
| Answers from a deleted page | Stale index; deletions must propagate, not just edits |
| Leaks another team's content | No access filter *at retrieval time* — filter before the model sees it, never after |
| Contradicts itself | Two versions of the same doc both retrieved; deduplicate and prefer the newest |

The access one is the serious one. **Authorisation belongs in the retrieval query**, scoped to the current user. A model asked to "only answer about documents the user can see" will comply approximately, which is not a security control.

## Evaluate the two halves separately

- **Retrieval:** for a set of real questions with known-good sources, was the right chunk in the top *k*? That is recall@k, and it is measurable without a model in the loop.
- **Generation:** given the right chunks, is the answer correct, grounded and properly cited?

Fixing generation when retrieval is the problem is the most common wasted week. The [eval discipline](/ai-dev/7) is the same otherwise: a frozen set from real traffic, scored per dimension, run on every change.

## Key takeaways

- RAG is a retrieval problem wearing a generation costume.
- Chunk on structure, retrieve hybrid, rerank — in that order of payoff.
- Filter by permission during retrieval, never by instruction.
- The UI owes the user sources, a real "not found" state, and citations that do not jump.
- Measure retrieval and generation separately, or you will fix the wrong half.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Why not just fine-tune?"** — Fine-tuning teaches behaviour and format, not facts you need current and citable. Documents change daily; an index update is cheap and a retrain is not.
- **"The answer is confidently wrong."** — Check whether the right chunk was retrieved at all before touching the prompt.
- **"How do you stop it leaking restricted content?"** — Scope the retrieval query to the user's permissions. Anything downstream of that is a request, not a control.

learnings.title: Agentic tooling in the dev loop
learnings.source: user request: AI-assisted development interview questions
learnings.answer:
The difference between a chat window and an agent is that the agent **acts**: it reads your files, edits them, runs your tests and iterates on what it sees. That changes what you have to be good at.

## What changes

| Chat assistant | Agentic tool |
| --- | --- |
| You paste context | It reads the repo |
| You copy the answer back | It edits files directly |
| You run the code | It runs the tests and reacts to failures |
| Wrong answer costs a paste | Wrong answer costs a diff across twelve files |
| You review one snippet | You review a change set |

The leverage is real and so is the failure mode: an agent that misunderstands the goal produces a *consistent, plausible* wrong change everywhere, rather than one obviously wrong function.

## How to run one well

**Scope the task like a ticket.** "Fix the flaky test in `useColumnWidths.test.js` — it fails when two resizes land in the same frame" beats "fix the tests". A narrow, verifiable goal is the single biggest quality lever.

**Give it a way to check itself.** A failing test, a type error, a reproduction command. An agent with a red signal to chase converges; an agent with only prose to satisfy drifts.

**Put the conventions in the repo.** `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` carries the package manager, the test command, the layering rules and the things you have already rejected — the same [context engineering](/ai-dev/3) argument, except it now applies to every file the agent touches.

**Keep the change reviewable.** One concern per run. Ask for a commit per logical step. A 40-file diff you cannot review is not a productivity gain, it is deferred debt with a plausible face.

**Read the diff, not the summary.** The summary is a claim about the diff. They are usually consistent; the interesting cases are exactly when they are not.

## The permission question

An agent that edits files and runs commands needs boundaries, and the sensible defaults are boring:

- **Version control is the safety net.** Never run one on a dirty tree you care about; commit or stash first, then the diff is the whole record.
- **Read-only by default, approve writes** while you are learning what a given task looks like.
- **Never auto-approve anything destructive** — force pushes, migrations, `rm -rf`, deploys, anything that spends money.
- **Sandbox or scope the working directory**, especially for anything driven by content you did not write.
- **Secrets stay out of the environment** it can read. Assume anything readable is read.
- **Treat fetched content as untrusted.** A page, an issue comment or a dependency's README can contain instructions; that is [prompt injection](/ai-dev/7), and an agent with tools is the case where it actually costs something.

## Where it is worth it, and where it is not

**Worth it:** mechanical migrations across many files, adding tests to untested code, chasing a failing test with a tight loop, dependency upgrades with a real test suite behind them, and orienting in an unfamiliar repo.

**Not worth it:** anything where the hard part is the decision, work you cannot review, a codebase with no tests (nothing to converge against), and small precise edits — describing them costs more than making them. Same boundary as [when not to reach for it](/ai-dev/4), pushed harder because the blast radius is bigger.

## The interview answer

> "It moves the bottleneck. Writing code stops being the constraint and reviewing it becomes one, so I run it on narrow, verifiable tasks with a red test to chase, keep the diffs small, and read every hunk. On a clean git tree, because that is the undo button."

## Key takeaways

- Agents act, so a misunderstanding becomes a consistent wrong change, not an obvious one.
- Narrow the task, give it a signal to converge on, keep the diff reviewable.
- Commit first; git is the safety net that makes the rest recoverable.
- Untrusted content plus tools is the real injection risk.
- You still own every line that lands.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you review a large agent-written change?"** — By behaviour and by pattern: the hunks that differ from their neighbours, plus a test that fails without the change. And I would rather have asked for smaller commits in the first place.
- **"What would you never let it do unattended?"** — Migrations, deploys, force pushes, anything spending money, and anything against production data.
- **"Has it made your team faster?"** — On mechanical work, clearly. The honest caveat is that review capacity became the constraint, so smaller PRs and stricter CI were the actual enabling change.
